edges.description: Prematurely activated intrapancreatic trypsin reaches the acinar cell through proteolytic autodigestion of the gland's own contents. The link type is indirect because that autodigestive step is not a node here, and because the primacy of trypsin in it is disputed by the same review that supplies the pathway - the refuting item below is on this edge as well as on the node, since it bears on whether the edge carries the disease or only accompanies it.
intermediate_mechanisms: Active intrapancreatic trypsin activates the other digestive proenzymes, and the resulting proteolysis digests the acinar cell that produced them.

edges.description: Ductal obstruction from inspissated secretions exposes the upstream acinar tissue to repeated injury.
intermediate_mechanisms: Failure of ductal fluid and bicarbonate secretion leaves protein plugs and stones in the duct, obstructing outflow from the acinus upstream.
edges.source: Impaired Ductal Chloride and Bicarbonate Secretion

edges.description: Repeated acinar injury is what activates the pancreatic stellate cells whose collagen deposition the fibrosis node models, so the injury node is upstream of fibrosis rather than parallel to it.
intermediate_mechanisms: Injured acinar tissue releases growth factors, cytokines and oxidant stress that activate pancreatic stellate cells.

edges.description: Pain in chronic pancreatitis begins as nociceptive input from the inflamed gland and is sustained by sensitization of the peripheral and central nervous system; the edge is marked indirect because the entry does not model that neural step as a node of its own.
intermediate_mechanisms: Nociceptive input from the inflamed pancreas drives peripheral and central sensitization, so the pain becomes neuropathic rather than purely nociceptive.

edges.description: Replacement of acinar parenchyma by fibrotic tissue is how the exocrine compartment is lost, which is the deficit the exocrine insufficiency node models.
The same fibrotic replacement destroys islet tissue, producing the endocrine deficit; the islet loss is described as slow and later in the course than the exocrine loss.
Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency causes fat malabsorption, manifesting as steatorrhea.
Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and malnutrition contribute to weight loss.
intermediate_mechanisms: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency causes maldigestion and malnutrition.

edges.description: Chronic pancreatitis-associated endocrine pancreatic damage manifests as pancreatogenic diabetes mellitus.

Alcohol is the commonest cause and acts on the acinar cell itself, which is why this link is direct. Graded partial because the sentence available describes a cohort assembled from patients who already had alcoholic pancreatitis; it presupposes the aetiology rather than demonstrating it.

Smoking brings the disease forward and hastens its structural endpoints, and it does so independently of how much alcohol a patient drinks. Recorded as exacerbating rather than triggering, in contrast to the alcohol link into this same node, because every cited figure measures acceleration of an established alcoholic pancreatitis rather than initiation.

nodes.description: The trypsin-independent, ductal arm of susceptibility. CFTR is the apical chloride channel of the pancreatic duct cell and is central to ductal bicarbonate transport; when that transport fails, ductal secretions are not flushed and alkalinized normally, protein plugs and stones form, and the duct becomes a site of obstruction and injury. CFTR variants are the inherited route into this node and are the second most frequent genetic finding in the chronic-pancreatitis cohort cited in this entry's genetic section; the same ductal dysfunction also arises non-genetically, through cytoplasmic mislocalization of wild-type CFTR, which the cited review reports across alcoholic, idiopathic, obstructive and autoimmune chronic pancreatitis.

nodes.description:
The trypsin-dependent arm of genetic susceptibility to chronic pancreatitis. Trypsinogen is normally activated only in the duodenum; intrapancreatic conversion to trypsin is held in check by the Kazal-type inhibitor SPINK1 and by chymotrypsin C (CTRC), which degrades trypsinogen in concert with trypsin. PRSS1 gain-of-function variants raise intrapancreatic trypsin both by accelerating trypsinogen autoactivation and by making trypsinogen less susceptible to CTRC-dependent degradation, and loss of CTRC removes the same degradative step. This is the pathway the three protease-balance genes curated in this entry (PRSS1, CTRC, SPINK1) share, and the reason they are modelled on one node rather than separately.
The node asserts the pathway, not its causal primacy. The review cited here concludes that intrapancreatic trypsin is at most a mediator of pancreatitis responses rather than the initiating culprit, and that whether loss of SPINK1 changes trypsin activity in the pancreas is still unknown. Both statements are carried as refuting evidence below, so the node is not read as a stronger claim than its sources support.
